extracted.intended_audience: essayists, satirists, and general writers of prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writers on the ethical and stylistic handling of ridicule, lampoon, epitaphs, and public inscriptions; focuses on when satire is harmful and how memorials should represent their subjects. Emphasises tempering wit with humanity and ensuring representations are accurate and tasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid secret stabs to reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing that more betrays a base, ungenerous Spirit, than the giving of secret Stabs to a Man's Reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lampoons and Satyrs, that are written with Wit and Spirit, are like poison'd Darts, which not only inflict a Wound, but make it incurable. Consider that an Injury is not to be measured by the Notions of him that gives, but of him that receives it; private and anonymous attacks produce secret shame and enduring sorrow. Do not expose private persons or families to derision for private faults or unlucky features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper wit with virtue and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: So pernicious a thing is Wit, when it is not tempered with Virtue and Humanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wit untempered leads to attacking Virtue and Merit themselves; therefore ridicule should be moderated by compassion and moral sense. Writers should avoid making praise-worthy qualities the objects of buffoonry and should weigh the real harm their satire does.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure injury by the receiver's perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man should consider, that an Injury is not to be measured by the Notions of him that gives, but of him that receives it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a lampoon seems trivial to the author, the affected person may experience lasting disgrace or prefer losing money or life to public infamy. Writers should assess likely impact on the target, not just their own intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indiscreet levity is more harmful than malice
rubrics_metrics.description: An indiscreet Man is more hurtful than an ill-natured one; for as the former will only attack his Enemies, and those he wishes ill to, the other injures indifferently both Friends and Foes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of heedless or inconsiderate writers who, out of a desire to be witty or distinguished, sacrifice friends' reputations. Curb ambitions for raillery that lead to careless personal attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer generosity or civility in responding to satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Generous or civil treatment of one's satirist can have a reforming effect and sometimes convert enemies into friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Julius Caesar invited Catullus to supper and made him a friend; Cardinal Mazarin treated Quillet kindly and later rewarded him, resulting in removal of offending passages. Rather than retaliation or cruelty, measured civility may neutralize satire and improve relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anonymous or hidden attacks (accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a greater Gratification to a barbarous and inhuman Wit, than to stir up Sorrow ... at the same time that he remains unseen and undiscovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anonymous 'arrows that fly in the dark' evade responsibility and enable malicious harm. Writers should avoid hiding behind anonymity to wound reputations; accountability is an ethical requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not satirize the undeserving (private persons, families, women)
rubrics_metrics.description: An Innocent young Lady shall be exposed, for an unhappy Feature. A Father of a Family turn'd to Ridicule, for some domestick Calamity. A Wife be made uneasy all her Life, for a misinterpreted Word or Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire that targets private, non-public figures or that amplifies trivial personal faults into public shame is morally wrong. Reserve sharper satire for public figures or clearly culpable subjects; avoid attacking persons whose private circumstances make public ridicule particularly harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs and monuments should be accurate and well-judged
rubrics_metrics.description: Monuments and inscriptions should be submitted to Men of Learning and Genius before they are put in Execution; many epitaphs are extravagant or inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review public memorials for appropriateness: avoid extravagant praise that would embarrass the deceased, ensure inscriptions actually celebrate meaningful actions (not merely manner of death), and choose imagery that reflects the true character (avoid dressing a rough admiral as a beau). Good epitaphs honour both the living and the dead and reflect national taste and antiquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear language in public inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are others so excessively modest, that they deliver the Character of the Person departed in Greek or Hebrew, and by that Means are not understood once in a Twelve-month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure or foreign-language inscriptions that render a monument meaningless to the general public; clarity and accessibility are virtues in public commemorative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should fit the subject (authentic iconography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir Cloudesly Shovel's Monument ... instead of the brave rough English Admiral, ... he is represented ... by the Figure of a Beau.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and inscription should represent the true nature and deeds of the person commemorated. Avoid fashionable falsehoods or stylish depictions that mischaracterise the subject; aim for authenticity and appropriate symbolism (e.g., naval ornaments for admirals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inducing unnecessary fear or hypochondria in didactic writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fear of Death often proves mortal, and sets People on Methods to save their Lives, which infallibly destroy them. This ... may be applied to those Multitudes of Imaginary Sick Persons that break their Constitutions by Physick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing about health or prescribing regimens, avoid promoting groundless fears and over-medicalisation. Encourage reasonable care for health, but not a life consumed by anxious schemes to preserve it; emphasise living well rather than merely prolonging life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fable and anecdote to illustrate moral points
rubrics_metrics.description: I shall tell him a short Fable ... (Jupiter and the country-man who mismanaged the weather) used to make the point that one should not over-control life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concise fables and historical anecdotes to exemplify moral lessons and make abstract cautions (about satire, health, or vanity) more memorable and persuasive. Ensure the illustrative story is clearly tied to the lesson.
